text:
🦉 Immunology Patent Signals

October 1–31, 2026 | Monthly Immunology Patent Digest | UTC

October's patent disclosures reveal a shift in how researchers are trying to improve immunotherapy.

More powerful immune activation is no longer the only objective. Several inventions seek to control where T cells activate, separate expansion from tumor recognition, overcome vascular and metabolic barriers, or identify toxicity before treatment begins.

We selected 12 patent developments that illustrate these approaches. Some contain intriguing experimental evidence. Others remain technical proposals with substantial questions unanswered.

The most interesting theme is how differently developers are addressing the same problem: making immune cells effective without making them dangerously indiscriminate.

📜 1. When Removing a Signal Might Improve CAR-T Function

CAR designs usually add signaling domains to increase T-cell activation. An October patent takes an unexpectedly different direction.

Vanudis describes an accessory immune-cell recruiting receptor that uses the transmembrane region of an adhesion molecule, while weakening or completely removing its intracellular costimulatory signaling domain.

The document describes experimental findings that challenge the assumption that additional intracellular signaling is always necessary for improved antigen sensitivity.

The scientific question is important: can receptor architecture and membrane organization improve immune-cell function without simply adding more activating signals?

That would offer a different route to improving engineered T cells. But evidence from patent examples is not equivalent to independent clinical validation, and the precise contribution of membrane geometry versus other receptor properties still requires investigation.

Vanudis · WO2026209887A1 · October 8 · International patent application
https://t.co/Y40mHSuVI8

📜 2. T-Cell Engagers That Respond to Tumor Acidity

A bispecific antibody can recognize a tumor antigen and recruit a T cell. The difficulty is that tumor-associated antigens are rarely exclusive to cancer.

BigHat Biosciences proposes another layer of selectivity: CEACAM6×CD3 T-cell engagers engineered to bind more strongly in acidic conditions.

In one disclosed binding example, CD3 affinity improved approximately tenfold, from around 200 nM at pH 7.4 to 20 nM at pH 6.0. The platform also explores low-affinity, high-avidity CEACAM6 recognition.

Rather than relying entirely on antigen expression, the design attempts to exploit a property of the tumor environment.

The distinction matters. Acid-sensitive binding could help discriminate between tissues, but it does not automatically establish tumor-specific killing or a favorable therapeutic window. Normal tissues can also experience acidic conditions, and clinical safety has not been demonstrated.

BigHat Biosciences · WO2026222338A1 · October 22 · International patent application
https://t.co/l9zIuYyfZG

📜 3. Expanding CAR-T Cells Without Their Tumor Antigen

One of October's most interesting inventions separates CAR-T expansion from direct recognition of the tumor.

Innovative Cellular Therapeutics describes a system containing three populations: PAP-targeted CAR-T cells, CD19-targeted CAR-T cells, and CD19-positive B cells.

The CD19 CAR-T/B-cell interaction provides costimulatory and cytokine signals that support expansion of the PAP-targeted cells, even without engagement of their own tumor antigen.

In the patent's mouse experiments, circulating PAP CAR-T cells expanded more than fivefold relative to PAP CAR-T treatment alone at day 14. The combined system also improved tumor control in a prostate cancer xenograft model.

This challenges an important assumption about adoptive cell therapy: that therapeutic T cells must repeatedly encounter their target antigen to expand effectively.

But the three-component system adds manufacturing and dosing complexity. Its apparent advantages in memory-associated phenotypes and exhaustion markers still need clinical testing.

Innovative Cellular Therapeutics · US20260325581A1 · October 22 · Published US application
https://t.co/l9FHdmkdrM

📜 4. Engineering CAR-T Cells Inside the Patient

Stanford University proposes a targeted lentiviral platform designed to deliver CAR constructs directly to T cells.

The vector carries a modified VSV-G protein that does not bind the conventional LDL receptor, alongside T-cell-targeting binding fragments. It also encodes both a CAR and an IL-9 receptor.

The goal is to make gene delivery more selective and potentially generate therapeutic CAR-T cells in vivo rather than relying exclusively on centralized ex vivo manufacturing.

There is an important technical obstacle here. A gene-delivery system must reach the intended cells, avoid unwanted transduction, achieve adequate expression, and remain safe.

The patent describes a proposed solution to these problems; it does not establish that in vivo manufacturing is clinically equivalent to conventional CAR-T production.

Stanford University · WO2026226990A1 · October 29 · International patent application
https://t.co/CaE60Vjujd

📜 5. CAR-T Cells That Also Target the Tumor's Blood Supply

Destroying cancer cells is not the only challenge in solid tumors. Their abnormal vasculature can limit immune-cell access and reinforce an immunosuppressive microenvironment.

A patent from Massachusetts General Hospital describes CAR-T cells that also express a bispecific antibody targeting VEGF and angiopoietin-2.

The concept combines tumor-antigen recognition with local interference in two pathways involved in vascular remodeling.

This is a different kind of CAR-T armoring. Rather than giving the cells another cytotoxic receptor, the design aims to change conditions around the tumor.

Whether simultaneous VEGF/Ang2 blockade improves trafficking, efficacy, or safety compared with established approaches remains an experimental question. The patent itself cannot establish a clinical advantage.

The General Hospital Corporation · WO2026226941A1 · October 29 · International patent application
https://t.co/1djuqzngH7

📜 6. Two Receptor Signals, Two Opposing CAR-T Outcomes

Not all immune receptors contribute equally to CAR-T persistence.

Kite Pharma's October application describes engineering TIGIT and CD27 pathways to improve cell function.

The document includes analyses of CAR-T products and clinical outcomes from subsets of the ZUMA-1, ZUMA-6, and ZUMA-7 studies. Higher CD27-related signaling features were associated with durable responses, whereas TIGIT-associated interactions were linked to progression.

The proposed engineering strategies include reducing TIGIT expression, introducing switch receptors, strengthening CD27 signaling, and selecting particular T-cell populations during manufacturing.

The interesting idea is that CAR-T performance may depend as much on the balance of inhibitory and supportive signals as on antigen recognition.

Yet associations in patient samples do not establish that engineering these pathways will improve survival. That requires prospective intervention studies.

Kite Pharma · WO2026226640A1 · October 29 · International patent application
https://t.co/qFQoB2zjFX

📜 7. Can CAR-T Neurotoxicity Be Predicted Before Infusion?

Most CAR-T safety assessments focus on patient characteristics, treatment exposures, and clinical changes after infusion.

Seattle Children's proposes looking directly at protein-interaction networks within the therapeutic cells.

Its patent describes biosignatures intended to distinguish cell products associated with neurotoxicity or cytokine release syndrome, potentially informing prediction or preventive intervention.

The idea is appealing because conventional cytotoxicity assays may miss cellular features that contribute to toxicity in patients.

The central unanswered question is predictive performance. Without independent prospective validation, a molecular signature cannot be assumed to reliably identify which patients will develop ICANS or severe CRS.

Seattle Children's Research Institute · WO2026218003A2 · October 15 · International patent application; accessible abstract
https://t.co/3qqvMTdo4w

📜 8. When Immunotherapy Becomes an Alternative to Surgery

An October application from Memorial Sloan Kettering covers methods of treating selected nonmetastatic mismatch-repair-deficient solid tumors without surgery.

The disclosed approaches include PD-1 blockade alone or combined with CTLA-4 inhibition, with clinical complete response forming part of the claimed treatment strategy.

The important development is not the discovery of PD-1 inhibition. It is the attempt to define and protect specific organ-preserving treatment methods.

This raises questions about patient selection, duration of response, surveillance, and the evidence needed before surgery can safely be omitted.

A patent application does not answer those clinical questions. Nor does publication of the claims represent regulatory authorization for a particular nonsurgical treatment strategy.

Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center · WO2026226924A2 · October 29 · International patent application
https://t.co/x9e7vO4Be7

📜 9. Selecting Patients for Dual PD-1/VEGF-Pathway Inhibition

Blocking PD-1 and VEGF-related signaling can alter both immune suppression and the tumor microenvironment. But benefit varies considerably between cancer types and patients.

Summit Therapeutics' October application describes baseline tumor biomarkers for selecting or guiding treatment involving PD-1 inhibition alongside VEGFR-pathway inhibition.

The potential value is straightforward: a combination therapy becomes more useful if clinicians can identify the patients most likely to benefit.

The difficult part is proving that a marker is predictive rather than merely prognostic. Clinical use would require defined assays, reproducible thresholds, and validation showing that marker-guided treatment improves decisions.

Summit Therapeutics · WO2026208876A1 · October 8 · International patent application
https://t.co/KRCNNbvZjx

📜 10. Borrowing Antimicrobial Immunity to Attack Tumors

What happens if cancer immunotherapy recruits an immune response normally directed against infection?

IMMREJ describes therapeutic approaches that introduce or exploit microbial antigenic features to generate an anti-infection-like T-cell response within tumors or metastatic sites.

The proposed strategy combines this response with other cancer immunotherapies.

Its appeal is that an existing or inducible antimicrobial immune response might be redirected toward cancer. Its weakness is equally important: efficient immune priming does not guarantee selective tumor killing, durable control, or acceptable inflammation.

The accessible disclosure establishes the proposed method, not clinical proof of synergy.

IMMREJ · WO2026218097A1 · October 22 · International patent application
https://t.co/ajIRPoYKf7

📜 11. Making Cancer Vaccines More Immunogenic Without More Reactogenicity

Immune stimulation presents a familiar problem in vaccine engineering: the same delivery system that activates useful immunity may also cause unwanted inflammation.

HDT Bio's October disclosure describes nanoparticles carrying nucleic acids and regulatory elements, including microRNA-binding sites, intended to influence reactogenicity and promote innate and adaptive immune responses.

Potential applications include therapeutic vaccines against cancer.

The technical idea is to engineer the delivery platform and its biological regulation together, rather than treating delivery as a passive transport problem.

The decisive tests will be whether reduced reactogenicity is accompanied by sufficient antigen-specific immunity, reproducible delivery, and clinically relevant antitumor activity.

HDT Bio · WO2026221982A2 · October 22 · International patent application; accessible abstract
https://t.co/c19hiBaKrp

📜 12. Dual-Target CARs: A Patent Grant, Not a New Discovery

October also brought an actual US patent grant covering a bispecific CAR directed against CD20 and BCMA.

AbelZeta's patent defines particular antigen-binding regions, their sequences, and their arrangement within the receptor. The disclosed applications include cancer and autoimmune disease.

Its significance is different from the preceding applications. This is a legal-status development: the US patent was granted on October 6, after an earlier application publication in May 2025.

The distinction is worth emphasizing. A granted patent protects specific allowed claims; it does not prove clinical efficacy or establish exclusive control over every possible CD20/BCMA combination.

AbelZeta · US12751973B2 · October 6 · Granted US patent; earlier public disclosure
https://t.co/OSyxXPyy6U

💡What These Patents Tell Us About the Direction of Immunotherapy

Three broader conclusions emerge from this selection.

First, control is becoming as important as potency.

The Vanudis, BigHat, Kite, and Seattle Children's disclosures approach immune activation from different directions: receptor architecture, environmental selectivity, intracellular signaling, and toxicity prediction. Their common objective is to improve useful activity without unnecessarily increasing harmful activity.

They are not interchangeable technologies, and their evidence comes from different experimental settings. But together they expose a limitation of simply pursuing stronger immune stimulation.

Second, the boundary between the therapeutic cell and its environment is becoming less rigid.

The Massachusetts General Hospital platform couples CAR recognition with vascular targeting. Stanford proposes targeted gene delivery directly to T cells. The CoupledCAR system uses additional immune-cell populations to support expansion without the tumor antigen.

These approaches differ fundamentally in complexity. One modifies the tumor environment, another changes where cell engineering happens, and a third changes how therapeutic cells receive growth signals.

None can yet be declared superior. Each solves one problem while introducing others involving specificity, manufacturability, control, or safety.

Third, patent disclosures are advancing across several levels of evidence — and those levels must not be confused.

Some documents contain comparative binding experiments, cellular assays, or animal-model results. Others primarily define proposed treatment methods or biomarker strategies. A patent grant adds legal certainty to particular claims, not biological validation.

For the field, the key distinction is between an invention that can be described, a mechanism that can be demonstrated, and a treatment that improves patient outcomes.

October's disclosures offer numerous ideas worth testing. The next decisive advances will come from determining which of those ideas survive rigorous comparative experiments and, eventually, clinical trials.

Etymology & Origin
Latin Root: Patricius is derived from pater, the Latin word for "father." In ancient Rome, the patricii (patricians) were members of the original ruling aristocratic class.
Christian Popularization: The name spread widely because of the 5th-century Saint Patrick, the Romanized Briton born Sucat who was captured by Irish raiders, escaped, and later returned as a bishop to Christianize Ireland.
Irish Forms: In Irish Gaelic, the name is rendered as Pádraig (or older forms like Patraicc). Historically, it was rarely used as an everyday given name in Ireland for centuries because it was considered too sacred to honor the saint lightly, though it became common after the 17th century.

The word "patrack" (more accurately spelled patîkr or patikar in ancient Middle-Eastern contexts) does not have a Babylonian origin, but is instead an Old Iranian word meaning "sculpture" or "image" that entered Jewish Babylonian Aramaic and Biblical Aramaic via cultural and linguistic contact.
Linguistic Evolution
Proto-Iranian root: Derived from patikárah, meaning a likeness, model, or sculpted image.
Aramaic adoption: Passed into Biblical Aramaic as פתכר (ptkr, meaning sculpture or idol) and Jewish Babylonian Aramaic as פתיכרי (ptkrʾ / pṯaḵrā).

About The Site:
Needless to say, St. Peter's Square (Piazza San Pietro) is the large circular plaza located in front of St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican City. Current St. Peter's Square was designed by Giovanni Lorenzo Bernini, and completed in 1667, have a width of 200 meters, depth is 165 meters, surrounded by the columns of the corridor. We can see the panoramic landscape of the square from the top of Basilica, which was designed by Michelangelo Buonarroti. It's worth to toil up to the Cupola (Dome). Although we can use the elevator until the middle way, but it's always crowded, and we must climb the narrow staircase of 320 steps after getting off the elevator. So, I walked up to the top without using the elevator.

How To Get There:
The entrance of Vatican City is about 400 meters south of Ottaviano Station on Metro Line "A". We wouldn't lose the way because many people are walking toward the Vatican City. Among them, some people are heading to the ticket office of Vatican Museum. In such a case, we should proceed in the opposite direction of the line along with the wall of Vatican City, then we can see the entrance. The obelisk majestically stands at the center of the square.
If we see the obelisk only, we may visit here at any time. However I recommend to climb up to the Cupola of St. Peter's. But we will receive the security inspection, and the people make a long waiting line in the daytime. So, visiting early in the morning is better. Also, visiting Vatican Museums is recommended. The admission ticket for the Museums, and the Sistine Chapel (Cappella Sistina) where there are the "Last Judgment" and the ceiling paintings is a set, and is available on the day. However, it takes more than 2 hours waiting line to obtain it, so purchasing online is recommended.

About The Obelisk:
The Provenance: The provenance of this obelisk is not well clarified.
According to one source, "The Natural History" authored by Pliny the Elder (Plinius) (An ancient Roman natural historian in AD 1st century), Nuncoreus, a son of Pharaoh Sesostris I (or Kheperkare Senusret I) (Pharaoh of Middle Kingdom, 12th Dynasty, reigned in 20th century BC) erected a pair of obelisk (2 obelisks) at the Temple in Heliopolis in token of his thanks for having recovered from blindness. One another obelisk (100 cubits high) still remains. [The Natural History, Volume 36, Chapter 15]
However, The stories in "The Natural History" is often a fake, but contains a lot of interesting fantastic stories. Hence we cannot acknowledge all the contents are fact, and must handle this carefully.
"The Natural History" doesn't refer to the location where the (pair of) obelisks were erected, and "Nuncoreus" doesn't exist in the history.
On the other hand, "Histories" ("historiai") authored by Herodotus (An ancient Greek historian in 5th century BC), King Pheron (Pharaoh Pheros) erected a pair of obelisk (2 obelisks) at the Temple in Heliopolis in token of his thanks for having recovered from blindness. [Histories, Volume 2, Section 111]
Since these stories are quite similar, Pliny the Elder might have copied from Herodotus' "Histories".
Pheros may be a common noun as the spelling of "pharaoh" and "pheros" are similar and this might be a derivative of "pharaoh".
According to another source, "The obelisk was quarried in Aswan in the era of Amenemhet II (Middle Kingdom, 12th Dynasty, 20th century BC), and erected at the Temple of Sun in Heliopolis.

However, the critical questions exist. This obelisk does not have the usual hieroglyph. It's hardly to believe the obelisk without hieroglyph was made in the time of Middle Kingdom, 12th Dynasty, in 20th century BC. It's also hardly to believe that Ramses II (13th century BC) overlooked it, and didn't make it as his own obelisk. Also, the current obelisk in Heliopolis has hieroglyph, but the Pharaoh name is Senusret I (Sesostris I), not Nuncoreus.

In anyway, this obelisk was brought to Alexandria and erected at the Julian Forum in Alexandria by Gaius Cornelius Gallus, the first Roman prefect of Egypt under Octavianus (the first Roman Emperor Augustus [reigned 27 BC - AD 14]), and was taken by Roman Emperor Caligula in AD 37, for Rome, and erected it as a spina of the Caligula Circus, later the Nero Circus (Circus Gai et Neronis, or the Vatican Circus).

In the creation myth of the Heliopolitan form of ancient Egyptian religion, Benben was the mound that arose from the primordial waters (Nu), and upon which the creator deity Atum settled. The Benben stone is associated with the top stone of a pyramid, which is called a pyramid's pyramidion (or benbenet). It is also related to the obelisk.

Primeval mound
In the Pyramid Texts, e.g. Utterances 587 and 600, Atum himself is at times referred to as "mound". It was said to have turned into a small pyramid, located in Heliopolis (Egyptian: Annu or Iunu), within which Atum was said to dwell. Other cities developed their own myths of the primeval mound. At Memphis, the god Tatenen, an earth god and the origin of "all things in the shape of food and viands, divine offers, all good things", was the personification of the primeval mound.

Benben stone
The Benben stone, named after the mound, was a sacred stone in the temple of Ra at Heliopolis (Egyptian: Annu or Iunu). It was the location on which the first rays of the sun fell. It is thought to have been the prototype for later obelisks, and the capstones of the great pyramids were based on its design. The capstone (the tip of the pyramid) is also called a pyramidion. In ancient Egypt, these were probably polished or clad so they shone in sunlight.[citation needed]

Many Benben stones, often carved with images and inscriptions, are found in museums around the world.

The bird deity Bennu, which was probably the inspiration for the phoenix, was venerated at Heliopolis, where it was said to be living on the Benben stone or on the holy willow tree.

According to Barry Kemp, the connection between the benben, the phoenix, and the sun may well have been based on alliteration: the rising, weben, of the sun sending its rays towards the benben, on which the bennu bird lives. Utterance 600, § 1652 of the Pyramid Texts speaks of Atum as you rose up, as the benben, in the Mansion of the Bennu in Heliopolis.[1]

Historical development
From the earliest times, the portrayal of Benben was stylized in two ways; the first was as a pointed, pyramidal form, which was probably the model for pyramids and obelisks. The other form was round-topped; this was probably the origin of Benben as a free standing votive object and an object of veneration.[2]

During the Fifth Dynasty, the portrayal of benben was formalized as a squat obelisk. Later, during the Middle Kingdom, this became a long, thin obelisk.

In the Amarna Period tomb of Panehesy, the benben is seen as a large, round-topped stela standing on a raised platform.[3]

Honored to meet a fellow traveler | Sen. Raphael Warnock had private meeting with the Pope
Georgia’s U.S. senator recalled his visit with the late Jorge Mario Bergolio at The Vatican last year.
By Andy Pierrotti and Tim Darnell
Published: Apr. 21, 2025 at 1:49 AM PDT| Updated: Apr. 21, 2025 at 5:40 AM PDT

ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) - Almost a year ago, U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock had a private meeting with Pope Francis at The Vatican

“I was deeply honored to meet not only the leader of the Catholic Church, but a fellow traveler,” Warnock said of the late Pontiff, who died Monday, April 21, 2025.

Warnock’s Papal visit was part of an April 2024 trip that involved briefings with the NATO Defense College and the World Food Programme.

Warnock said the two spoke and prayed about humanitarian crises across the globe, including Sudan, Ukraine and Palestinians in Gaza, still in the midst of a deadly conflict between Israel and Hamas. Warnock said Francis, with the help of an interpreter, told him he was in regular contact with a small congregation of Catholics in Gaza.

Jorge Mario Bergolio was born in Argentina Dec, 17, 1936, he was appointed Archbishop of Buenos Aires in 2001 and, taking the name of Pope Francis, was elected Supreme Pontiff on March 13, 2013.

The 88-year-old pope, who has chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man, was hospitalized several weeks ago for treatment of pneumonia.

Warnock has led Ebenezer Baptist Church - Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s former pastoral home - since 2005. Francis was elected by a papal conclave in 2013 at the age of 76, leading more than 1.3 billion Catholics across the globe.

Often revered and criticized as one of the most progressive popes in history, Francis had expressed support to address climate change, immigration and the LGBTQ community.

Warnock said the late Pontiff’s position on those issues demonstrated his focus on human decency. “That doesn’t mean we always land on the same side of every issue, but what I see in him is an effort to center human dignity,” Warnock said.

The senator said he and the late Pope shared a few laughs, but “I’ll keep that between us,” he said.

Martin Pradier, our Materials Analyst, joined BNN Bloomberg to discuss the recent gold rally and offer his three Hot Picks in the sector. He said the gold rally will continue but "at a slower pace," noting that interest rates will present a headwind. 

Martin likes Franco-Nevada because of its anticipated reopening of the Cobre Panama mine, a key catalyst. He also likes copper miner HudBay Minerals, noting it has the lowest cost structure, strongest growth and lowest valuation relative to peers. Interestingly, Martin explains why HudBay's cost structure is so low: "They're mining copper, but copper comes with a byproduct, and the product is gold," which covers all the copper mining costs. 

His third pick, Wheaton Precious Metals, has strong growth prospects and a fixed cost structure at a time when gold mining costs have risen 15-20% in recent quarters.

⬇️⬇️
On January 17, 2020, Jim Mullin, the teenage son of U.S. Senator Markwayne Mullin (R-OK), suffered a severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) during a high school wrestling accident. The injury left him unresponsive with an extremely low pulse for 26 hours. When he woke up, he experienced profound cognitive and motor deficits, requiring him to completely relearn how to walk, read, and perform basic functions. [1, 2, 3, 4]

The Extent of the Injury & Rehabilitation

Cognitive Regression: Jim went from operating at a high school academic level to a third-grade learning level practically overnight. He struggled with basic motor functions, short-term memory loss, and simple arithmetic. [1, 2, 3, 4]
Physical Impact: An elite, world-class youth wrestler, he lost muscle control and could no longer touch his nose or walk without shuffling his feet. [1, 2]
[1, 2, 3]Recovery: Jim underwent intensive, specialized rehabilitation at the Center for Neuro Skills in Bakersfield, California. Doctors initially estimated his recovery would take two to three years, but he was discharged to return home after nine months of progress in October 2020.

Connection to Donald Trump

The incident became a major focal point in March 2026 during Markwayne Mullin's Senate confirmation hearing for Secretary of Homeland Security. An emotional Mullin recounted how the tragedy forged his deep, unwavering personal loyalty to Donald Trump: [1, 2, 3]
Personal Outreach: Upon learning of the injury in 2020, Trump immediately called Mullin, offered his personal plane to transport Jim to the California neural rehab facility, and followed up with near-daily phone calls. [1, 2]
The Visit: In the middle of his 2020 reelection campaign, Trump flew to Bakersfield to visit Jim privately without any press or cameras. Mullin noted that Trump spent 15 minutes engaging with Jim, an interaction that significantly boosted the teenager's morale and visibly helped trigger his short-term memory recovery. [1, 2, 3]
